passages.title: Decision
passages.text: When the wind blew, waste paper hung on trees and fences. People were cut by broken glass that was thrown carelessly. Then one day, the tap dried up and our containers were empty. My father walked from house to house asking people to attend a village meeting. People gathered under a big tree and listened.

question.q: What happened right after the tap dried up?
choices: The wind blew the waste paper into the trees
Father asked everyone to come to a meeting
Everyone packed up and moved to a new village
The children cleaned up all the broken glass
question.evidence: My father walked from house to house asking people to attend a village meeting
question.explain: When the tap dried up, the father went from house to house asking people to meet.

passages.title: Goat, Dog, and Cow
passages.text: The driver was about to give Dog his change when Goat ran away without paying anything. The driver was very annoyed. He drove away without giving Dog his change. That is why, even today, Dog runs towards a car to peep inside and find the driver who owes him his change.

question.q: Why does Dog run toward cars, according to the story?
choices: He is looking for the driver who owes him change
He is trying to catch Goat, who ran away without paying
He likes to bark at the loud engines
He hopes to get a free ride into the next town
question.evidence: find the driver who owes him his change
question.explain: The driver drove off without giving Dog his change, so Dog still looks for him.

passages.title: Hen and Eagle
passages.text: After a good night's sleep, Hen had a brilliant idea. She began collecting the fallen feathers from all their bird friends. "Let's sew them together on top of our own feathers," she said. "Perhaps that will make it easier to travel." Eagle was the only one in the village with a needle, so she started sewing first. She made herself a pair of beautiful wings and flew high above Hen. Hen borrowed the needle but she soon got tired of sewing. She left the needle on the cupboard and went into the kitchen to prepare food for her children.

question.q: What did Hen do after she got tired of sewing?
choices: Asked all her bird friends to bring more feathers
Flew up high to join Eagle in the sky
Gave the needle back to Eagle and thanked her for it
Left the needle on the cupboard and went to cook
question.evidence: She left the needle on the cupboard and went into the kitchen
question.explain: Hen put the needle on the cupboard and went to the kitchen to make food.

passages.title: Why hippos have no hair
passages.text: One day, Rabbit was walking by the riverside. Hippo was there too, going for a stroll and eating some nice green grass. Hippo didn't see that Rabbit was there and she accidentally stepped on Rabbit's foot. Rabbit started screaming at Hippo, "You Hippo! Can't you see that you're stepping on my foot?"

question.q: How did Rabbit most likely feel when Hippo stepped on that foot?
choices: Proud that Hippo knew who Rabbit was
Happy to meet a friend by the river
Angry and hurt by the heavy Hippo
Too tired and sleepy to care at all
question.evidence: Rabbit started screaming at Hippo
question.explain: Rabbit screamed at Hippo, which shows Rabbit was hurt and angry.

passages.title: Hare Tricks Tortoise
passages.text: Once upon a time, there lived a tortoise, who had worked very hard during his entire life. When he retired, he received a nice lump sum of money. He decided that he would buy a big piece of land with the money, and become a farmer. News spread all over the village that Tortoise was looking for land to buy.

question.q: What did Tortoise plan to do with his money?
choices: Build a large new house in the village
Buy a big piece of land and farm it
Give it all away to his neighbours
Save it for a long trip to the sea
question.evidence: buy a big piece of land with the money, and become a farmer
question.explain: Tortoise wanted to buy land and become a farmer.

passages.title: Mod the Toad
passages.text: It was a cold and wet morning in the forest. Mod the little toad was tired of swimming in cold water. "I need to leave this place during the rainy season," she said to herself. "I want an adventure," said Mod to the terrapin. "I must find out about the world." "Be careful, don't leave the water for too long or your skin will dry out," warned the wise terrapin. At that time, toads still had smooth wet skin like frogs. Without water, their skins would become too dry.

question.q: Why did the terrapin tell Mod to be careful?
choices: Her skin would dry out away from the water
The forest was full of hungry snakes and birds
She might get lost and miss the rainy season
The cold water would make her very sick
question.evidence: don't leave the water for too long or your skin will dry out
question.explain: Toads then had smooth wet skin that would dry out without water.

passages.title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
passages.text: A few days later, the crocodile saw the monkey coming onto the island. He quietly climbed over the rock and carefully lay down on it and kept his face underwater. The monkey finished eating and was ready to go back. But the rock looked higher than usual, so he spoke to the rock, "Dear rock, you seem to have grown. Are you all right?"

question.q: Why did the rock look higher than usual?
choices: The monkey had piled stones on it
The rock was slowly growing bigger
The water in the river had gone down
The crocodile was lying on top of it
question.evidence: carefully lay down on it
question.explain: The crocodile had climbed onto the rock and lay on it, so it looked taller.

passages.title: Refiloe and the washed chickens
passages.text: It was the first wedding in the Tenane family, and Refiloe had never been so excited in her life. "I'm going to be Palesa's bridesmaid, with a new dress and shoes!" she said to her chickens. Refiloe told her chickens everything. Her father had given the chickens to her as a birthday present, and she loved them very much.

question.q: Who gave Refiloe her chickens?
choices: Palesa, the bride, as a thank-you gift
Her mother, for helping at the farm
Her father, as a birthday present
A neighbour, who was moving away
question.evidence: Her father had given the chickens to her as a birthday present
question.explain: The chickens were a birthday present from her father.

passages.title: Greedy Mairu
passages.text: Once upon a time, there lived a man called Mairu in Bubaali Village. He liked to eat meat so much. One day, the chairman of Bubaali village invited all the villagers to his wedding that was to take place at his home. Then Mairu also heard that there was another wedding in Nabuyanja village. "Ugh! ugh! ugh! Two parties on the same day!" Mairu imagined.

question.q: Why did Mairu cry "Ugh! ugh! ugh!"?
choices: He had not been invited to either of the weddings
He could not go to both feasts on the same day
He did not like the meat served at weddings
The other village was too far to walk to
question.evidence: Two parties on the same day!
question.explain: Mairu loved meat and wanted both parties, but they were on the same day.

passages.title: The Puppy That Did Not Bark
passages.text: Rinku was a little girl who lived in a big house with her parents and baby sister. She looked out into the garden and thought how wonderful it would be if she had a dog as her pet and play with him in the garden every evening. "Mummy, please get me a small puppy", she asked her mother. Her mother said, "I'm sorry Rinku, it is very difficult to take care of a pup."

question.q: What did Rinku wish she could do every evening?
choices: Play with a pet dog in the garden
Read stories to her little baby sister
Watch the birds from her bedroom window
Walk to the park with her mother
question.evidence: play with him in the garden every evening
question.explain: Rinku dreamed of playing with a pet dog in the garden every evening.

passages.title: Samira's Awful Lunch
passages.text: Shutting her tiffin box with a bang, Samira went to the school courtyard. A row of ants crawling along the wall said, "Samira, why aren't you eating your lunch like all the other children?" Samira said, "I don't like parathas. I don't like vegetables. I don't want any lunch." "Of course, one cannot eat vegetables," the ants agreed. They offered her the wing of a cockroach that they were carefully carrying and said, "Now try this, it is really delicious." "Oh no! I don't want any horrible cockroaches," said Samira and ran away to the garden.

question.q: Why did Samira run away to the garden?
choices: The ants had bitten her hand very hard
She wanted to share her lunch with friends
She was late for her lesson in the garden
She did not want to eat the cockroach wing
question.evidence: I don't want any horrible cockroaches
question.explain: The ants offered her a cockroach wing, and she did not want it.

passages.title: Tok Tok
passages.text: Tok-tok tok-tok! Raja Petuchand of Sonapur buried his head under the pillow. The butter chicken he had enjoyed a little too much last night was already giving him trouble. Now this awful noise! "Do you have to get the palace work done at this hour?" he grumbled to queen Suruchi. But she was snoring peacefully next to him in the king-sized bed, dreaming of the next palace festival. Tok-tok... tok-tok!

question.q: In this story, what does "grumbled" mean?
choices: laughed loudly at a very funny joke
sang a happy little song out loud
complained in a cross, unhappy way
whispered a kind secret very softly
question.evidence: he grumbled to queen Suruchi
question.explain: The king was upset by the noise, so he complained crossly.

passages.title: Grandpa Fish and the Radio
passages.text: Grandpa Fish was the head of the fish family. He was obeyed in most things, not just by the younger fish but also by the frog and tortoise families. But there was one thing over which he simply had no control: the family radio.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Venkatramana Gowda
source.note: Excerpt (pages 5-6). Shortened. Translated by Divaspathy Hegde.

question.q: What could Grandpa Fish not control?
choices: The younger fish
The family radio
The frog families
The water in the stream
question.evidence: one thing over which he simply had no control: the family radio
question.explain: He was obeyed in most things, but not about the radio.

passages.title: Gargi and Soapy
passages.text: "Gargi, come here wash your hands thoroughly," said Mother with a soap-box in her hand. "noooooo".....screamed and cried Gargi as if she saw a monster in the soap-box. She kicked Soapy so hard that he flew up and hit the ceiling of the bathroom. Soapy was scared of Gargi and fed up of her tantrums.

question.q: Who is Soapy?
choices: A bar of soap kept in the soap-box
Gargi's younger brother at home
A toy monster from under the bed
Gargi's pet kitten in the bathroom
question.evidence: a soap-box in her hand
question.explain: Mother held a soap-box, and Gargi kicked Soapy when told to wash.

passages.title: Under the Sea
passages.text: Underwater is amazing! Though it was a little difficult to get used to breathing, Rehan soon learnt the trick. He floated, swam and then dived in. He felt good. Ooooooh! It was fascinating to see all kinds of colourful fishes swimming in all directions! There were rocks, corals, flowers, plants,.... all surrounded by the blue sea. The plants were swaying gently as though they were talking.

question.q: In this story, "fascinating" means...
choices: hard to see clearly at all
scary and very dangerous
boring and much too quiet
very interesting to watch
question.evidence: It was fascinating to see all kinds of colourful fishes
question.explain: Rehan loved watching the colorful fish, so it was very interesting.

passages.title: Uncle Paul and the Pear-Tree
passages.text: UNCLE PAUL had just cut down a pear-tree in the garden. The tree was old, its trunk ravaged by worms, and for several years it had not borne any fruit. It was to be replaced by another. The children found their Uncle Paul seated on the trunk of the pear-tree. He was looking attentively at something. "One, two, three, four, five," said he, tapping with his finger upon the cross-section of the felled tree. What was he counting?

question.q: What was Uncle Paul most likely counting?
choices: The children waiting for him in the garden
The worms that had eaten their way into the trunk
The rings in the wood that show the tree's age
The pears the old tree had grown in past summers
question.evidence: tapping with his finger upon the cross-section of the felled tree
question.explain: He tapped the cut end of the trunk, where a tree's yearly rings show.

passages.title: Inside a Flower
passages.text: "Let us examine together this gillyflower. It has a calyx of four sepals and a corolla of four yellow petals. I take away these eight pieces. What is left now is the essential part; that is to say, the thing without which the flower could not fill its role and would be perfectly useless. Let us go carefully over this remaining part. You will find it well worth the trouble.

question.q: What does "essential" mean in this paragraph?
choices: the part that always falls off first
the part the flower cannot do without
the smallest and the least useful part
the prettiest and most colorful part
question.evidence: the thing without which the flower could not fill its role
question.explain: The text explains that the essential part is what the flower cannot do without.

passages.title: The Air Is a Great Drinker
passages.text: "In watering my garden," answered Jules, "I did not think I was watering the air more than anything else. But I see now: air is the great drinker. Of the contents of a watering-pot the plants take perhaps a handful; the air drinks up the rest. And that is why we have to do it all over again every day."

question.q: What has Jules learned about watering his garden?
choices: Most of the water he pours goes into the air
Watering once a week is plenty for plants
The garden needs no water on cloudy days
Plants drink up all of the water he gives them
question.evidence: Of the contents of a watering-pot the plants take perhaps a handful; the air drinks up the rest
question.explain: Jules sees that the air takes most of the water, so he must water daily.

passages.title: The Jumping Paper
passages.text: Uncle Paul took from his desk a stick of sealing-wax and rubbed it rapidly over his cloth sleeve; then he put it near a small piece of paper. The children were all eyes. Behold, the paper flies up and sticks to the sealing-wax. The experiment is repeated several times. Each time the paper rises unaided, starts off, and fastens on to the stick.

question.q: What did Uncle Paul do before he held the wax near the paper?
choices: He wrapped it up in a small sheet of paper
He warmed it gently over a candle flame
He dipped the stick into a glass of water
He rubbed it quickly on his cloth sleeve
question.evidence: rubbed it rapidly over his cloth sleeve
question.explain: First he rubbed the wax on his sleeve, then he put it near the paper.

passages.title: Spiders' Hunting Nets
passages.text: "Hiding-place!" exclaimed Jules; "yes, I think it is more than that. One day I heard, between the lilac branches, a little shrill noise-he-e-e-e! A blue fly was entangled in a cobweb and trying to escape. It was the fly that was making the noise with its fluttering. A spider ran from the bottom of the silken funnel, seized the fly, and carried it off to its hole, doubtless to eat it. Since then I have thought spiders' webs were hunting nets."

question.q: What does Jules now think spiders' webs are?
choices: They are only safe places for spiders to hide
They are cozy homes built for the blue flies
They are nets for catching insects to eat
They are made to keep the rain off the lilacs
question.evidence: I have thought spiders' webs were hunting nets
question.explain: After seeing the spider catch the fly, Jules thinks webs are hunting nets.

passages.title: A Baby's First Song
passages.text: WHEN a baby is perfectly healthy and has had enough to eat and has slept all it wants, then it hums a little tune to show how happy it is. To grown-ups this humming means nothing. It sounds like "goo-zum, goo-zum, goo-o-o-o-o," but to the baby it is perfect music. It is his first contribution to art.

source.name: The Story of Mankind (Hendrik Willem van Loon, 1921)
source.author: Hendrik Willem van Loon

question.q: Why does a healthy baby hum, according to the writer?
choices: To ask for something more to eat
To show everyone how happy it is
To call for a grown-up to come
Because it is tired and sleepy
question.evidence: it hums a little tune to show how happy it is
question.explain: The baby hums to show it is happy.

passages.title: The Man with the Saw
passages.text: Suppose that you were Champollion, and that you were examining a stack of papyrus sheets, all covered with hieroglyphics. Suddenly you came across a picture of a man with a saw. "Very well," you would say, "that means of course that a farmer went out to cut down a tree." Then you take another papyrus. It tells the story of a queen who had died at the age of eighty-two. In the midst of a sentence appears the picture of the man with the saw. Queens of eighty-two do not handle saws. The picture therefore must mean something else. But what?

source.name: The Story of Mankind (Hendrik Willem van Loon, 1921)
source.author: Hendrik Willem van Loon

question.q: Why must the picture of the man with the saw mean something else?
choices: An old queen would not be cutting down trees
The farmer in the first story was her son
Saws had not yet been invented in her time
Queens in Egypt were not allowed to read papyrus
question.evidence: Queens of eighty-two do not handle saws
question.explain: A story about an 82-year-old queen would not show her sawing, so the picture means something else.

passages.title: The Roman Empire Was an Accident
passages.text: THE Roman Empire was an accident. No one planned it. It "happened." No famous general or statesman or cut-throat ever got up and said "Friends, Romans, Citizens, we must found an Empire. Follow me and together we shall conquer all the land from the Gates of Hercules to Mount Taurus."

source.name: The Story of Mankind (Hendrik Willem van Loon, 1921)
source.author: Hendrik Willem van Loon

question.q: What is the main idea of this paragraph?
choices: The Romans conquered the land in one great war
The Roman Empire stayed very small and weak
One famous general carefully planned the whole empire
No one planned the Roman Empire; it just happened
question.evidence: No one planned it.
question.explain: The writer says the Roman Empire was an accident that just happened.

passages.title: The King and His Hawk
passages.text: On the king's wrist sat his favorite hawk; for in those days hawks were trained to hunt. At a word from their masters they would fly high up into the air, and look around for prey. If they chanced to see a deer or a rabbit, they would swoop down upon it swift as any arrow.

question.q: In this paragraph, "prey" means...
choices: the strap worn on the king's wrist
a short prayer said before a hunt
animals that are hunted for food
a nest built high up in a tree
question.evidence: look around for prey. If they chanced to see a deer or a rabbit
question.explain: Prey are animals, like deer and rabbits, that hawks hunt.

passages.title: King John and the Abbot
passages.text: "Very well, then," said the king, "I will give you something else to pay you for this merry joke. I will give you four pieces of silver every week as long as you live. And when you get home, you may tell the old abbot that you have brought him a free pardon from King John."

question.q: What did the king promise to give every week?
choices: A letter for the abbot
Four pieces of silver
Two bags of gold coins
Four loaves of bread
question.evidence: four pieces of silver every week as long as you live
question.explain: The king promised four pieces of silver every week for life.

passages.title: William Tell
passages.text: One day this tyrant set up a tall pole in the public square, and put his own cap on the top of it; and then he gave orders that every man who came into the town should bow down before it. But there was one man, named William Tell, who would not do this. He stood up straight with folded arms, and laughed at the swinging cap. He would not bow down to Gessler himself.

question.q: What kind of man was William Tell?
choices: Brave enough to stand up to an unfair ruler
Too tired to notice the cap on the pole
Afraid of Gessler and all his soldiers
Eager to do whatever the new ruler of the town said
question.evidence: He would not bow down to Gessler himself.
question.explain: He refused to bow and even laughed at the cap, which took courage.

passages.title: The Muddy Horseman
passages.text: One day some men were sitting by the door of a hotel in Baltimore. As they looked down the street they saw a horseman coming. He was riding very slowly, and both he and his horse were bespattered with mud.

question.q: What does "bespattered" mean in this paragraph?
choices: tired out and hungry from riding
tied to each other with a rope
dressed in fine, clean clothes
splashed and covered with spots
question.evidence: both he and his horse were bespattered with mud
question.explain: Bespattered with mud means splashed all over with mud.

passages.title: The Old Man at the Market
passages.text: In Richmond, Virginia, one Saturday morning, an old man went into the market to buy something. He was dressed plainly, his coat was worn, and his hat was dingy. On his arm he carried a small basket.

question.q: How was the old man dressed?
choices: In a long farmer's apron covered with mud
In a fine new suit and a tall shiny hat
Plainly, with a worn coat and a dingy hat
In a soldier's uniform with bright buttons
question.evidence: He was dressed plainly, his coat was worn, and his hat was dingy.
question.explain: The text says he was dressed plainly in a worn coat and dingy hat.

passages.title: The Whistle
passages.text: "Never mind, my child," said his mother, very kindly. "You are only a very little boy, and you will learn a great deal as you grow bigger. The lesson you have learned to-day is never to pay too dear for a whistle." Benjamin Franklin lived to be a very old man, but he never forgot that lesson.

question.q: What lesson did young Benjamin Franklin learn?
choices: Always to buy the biggest and best toy in the shop
Not to pay more for a thing than it is worth
Never to play music when others are near
To save his money until he was grown up
question.evidence: never to pay too dear for a whistle
question.explain: To pay too dear means to pay more than something is worth.

passages.title: The Boys and the Paddle Wheels
passages.text: After a great deal of tinkering and trying, they did succeed in making two paddle wheels. They were very rough and crude, but strong and serviceable. They fastened each of these wheels to the end of an iron rod which they passed through the boat from side to side. The rod was bent in the middle so that it could be turned as with a crank. When the work was finished, the old fishing boat looked rather odd, with a paddle wheel on each side which dipped just a few inches into the water. The boys lost no time in trying it.

question.q: What did the boys do after they made the two paddle wheels?
choices: Fastened each wheel to the end of an iron rod
Took the boat to show it to their teacher
Sold the old fishing boat to buy a new one
Painted both of the wheels a bright red color
question.evidence: They fastened each of these wheels to the end of an iron rod
question.explain: Next they fastened the wheels to an iron rod passed through the boat.

passages.title: John Randolph at the Inn
passages.text: A fine supper was prepared, and the innkeeper himself waited upon his guest. John Randolph ate in silence. The innkeeper spoke of the weather, of the roads, of the crops, of politics. But his surly guest said scarcely a word.

question.q: What does "surly" mean in this paragraph?
choices: very hungry and thirsty
sleepy and very tired
cheerful and chatty
rude and unfriendly
question.evidence: his surly guest said scarcely a word
question.explain: The guest would hardly speak to the kind innkeeper, which was rude.

passages.title: Peter Goes to School
passages.text: "Yes," replied Peter, "but there are lots and lots of things I would like to know about other people. If you please, I would like to come to school to you every day. You see, the more I learn about my neighbors, the better able I will be to take care of myself."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why does Peter want to come to school every day?
choices: His mother told him he had to go every day
He is lonely and wants other animals to play with
Knowing his neighbors will help keep him safe
He hopes to become a teacher himself someday
question.evidence: the more I learn about my neighbors, the better able I will be to take care of myself
question.explain: Peter says learning about his neighbors will help him take care of himself.

passages.title: Jumper Is Not Ashamed
passages.text: "I'm not ashamed of running," declared Jumper. "I may be ever so much bigger, but he is so quick I wouldn't stand the least chance in the world. When I suspect Shadow is about, I go somewhere else, the farther the better. If I could climb a tree like Chatterer, it would be different."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why does Jumper go somewhere else when Shadow is about?
choices: Jumper is ashamed of being so big and slow
Shadow is so quick Jumper would have no chance
Jumper is looking for a tall tree to climb
Shadow has told him to leave the woods for good
question.evidence: he is so quick I wouldn't stand the least chance in the world
question.explain: Jumper is bigger, but Shadow is so quick that running is safest.

passages.title: Creaker and the Eggs
passages.text: Creaker's yellow eyes began to twinkle. "That is a very personal question," said he. "I won't go so far as to say I steal eggs, but I've found that eggs are very good for my constitution and if I find a nest with nobody around I sometimes help myself to the eggs. You see the owner might not come back and then those eggs would spoil, and that would be a pity."

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What does Creaker's answer show?
choices: He does take eggs but makes excuses for it
He watches nests to keep the eggs safe for others
He only eats eggs that have already spoiled
He has never once touched another bird's egg
question.evidence: if I find a nest with nobody around I sometimes help myself to the eggs
question.explain: He admits he helps himself to eggs, then gives a reason to make it sound fine.

passages.title: Phoebes Under Bridges
passages.text: "Oh," replied Dear Me, "we Phoebes always have been fond of building under bridges. You see a place like this is quite safe. Then, too, we like to be near water. Always there are many insects flying around where there is water, so it is an easy matter to get plenty to eat. I left the shed at Farmer Brown's because that pesky cat up there discovered our nest last year, and we had a dreadful time keeping our babies out of her clutches. She hasn't found us down here, and she wouldn't be able to trouble us if she should find us."

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Where do Phoebes like to build their nests?
choices: Inside an old hollow stump
In sheds on a busy farm
High up in a tall maple tree
Under bridges near the water
question.evidence: we Phoebes always have been fond of building under bridges
question.explain: Dear Me says Phoebes are fond of building under bridges, near water.

passages.title: Whip-poor-will's Whiskers
passages.text: "Nobody asked you to swallow them. Nobody wants you to swallow them," snapped Jenny. "I don't know why a bird shouldn't have whiskers just as well as you, Peter Rabbit. Anyway, Whip-poor-will has them and that is all there is to it. It doesn't make any difference whether you believe in them or not, they are there. And I guess Whip-poor-will finds them just as useful as you find yours, and a little more so. I know this much, that if I had to catch all my food in the air I'd want whiskers and lots of them so that the insects would get tangled in them. I suppose that's what Whip-poor-will's are for."

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What does Jenny Wren think the whiskers are for?
choices: To feel its way through the dark woods
To keep its face warm in the winter
To help it catch insects while flying
To make it look more like a rabbit
question.evidence: so that the insects would get tangled in them
question.explain: Jenny says insects caught in the air would get tangled in the whiskers.

passages.title: Mr. Owl Takes What He Wants
passages.text: "Now when people are very big and very strong and afraid of nothing and nobody they are very apt to care for nothing and nobody but themselves. So it was with Mr. Owl. Whatever he saw that he wanted he took, no matter to whom it belonged, for there was no one to stop him.

source.name: Mother West Wind's Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1911)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What is this paragraph mostly about?
choices: How Mr. Owl learned to share with friends
How Mr. Owl took things that were not his
How Mr. Owl built his home in the forest
How Mr. Owl grew afraid of all the others
question.evidence: Whatever he saw that he wanted he took, no matter to whom it belonged
question.explain: Because he was big and fearless, Mr. Owl took whatever he wanted.

passages.title: Reddy Fox Shows Off
passages.text: Little Joe Otter was there, and Billy Mink and Jerry Muskrat and Happy Jack Squirrel, and of course Reddy Fox was there. Oh my, yes, of course Reddy Fox was there! Reddy Fox never misses a chance to show off. He was wearing his very newest red coat and his whitest waistcoat. He had brushed his tail till it looked very handsome, and every few minutes he would turn and admire it. Reddy Fox thought himself a very fine gentleman. He admired himself and he wanted every one else to admire him.

source.name: Mother West Wind's Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1911)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

choices: Reddy Fox showing off his fine looks
Reddy Fox hiding from the other animals
Reddy Fox teaching the others a game
Reddy Fox hunting for his breakfast
question.evidence: Reddy Fox never misses a chance to show off
question.explain: Most sentences tell how Reddy Fox dressed up and admired himself.

passages.title: The First Wolf Howl
passages.text: "One night he sat thinking about it. Gentle Mistress Moon looked down at him through the tree-tops, and something inside him urged him to tell her his troubles. He pointed his sharp nose up at her, opened his mouth and, because she was so far away, did his best to make her hear. That was the very first Wolf howl ever heard. There was something very lonely and shivery and terrible in the sound, and all who heard it shook with fear. Mr. Wolf didn't know this, but he did know that he felt better for howling. So every night he pointed his nose up at Mistress Moon and howled.

source.name: Mother West Wind 'How' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1916)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why did Mr. Wolf point his nose up and howl?
choices: He was hungry and calling his family to supper
He wanted to scare the other animals away
He was angry that she kept hiding behind the trees
She was far away, and he wanted her to hear him
question.evidence: because she was so far away, did his best to make her hear
question.explain: He wanted to tell Mistress Moon his troubles, and she was far away.

passages.title: King Bear's Gift
passages.text: "One day old King Bear gave little Mr. Squirrel six big, fat nuts. You see, old King Bear didn't care for nuts himself, not the kind with the hard shells, anyway, so he really wasn't as generous as he seemed, which is the way with a great many people. It is easy to give what you don't want yourself. Little Mr. Squirrel bowed very low and thanked old King Bear in his best manner. He really didn't want those nuts, for his stomach was full at the time, but it wouldn't do to refuse a gift from the king. So he took the nuts and pretended to be delighted with them.

source.name: Mother West Wind 'How' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1916)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why was King Bear not as generous as he seemed?
choices: He took the nuts back the very next day
He gave Mr. Squirrel only one nut, not six
He gave away nuts he did not want himself
He made Mr. Squirrel pay for the nuts
question.evidence: It is easy to give what you don't want yourself.
question.explain: King Bear didn't care for hard-shelled nuts, so giving them cost him nothing.

passages.title: Mischief and Trouble
passages.text: "One morning the very imp of mischief seemed to get into old Mr. Possum's head. Yes, Sir, it certainly did seem that way. And when you see Mischief trotting along the Lone Little Path, if you look sharp enough, you'll see Trouble following at his heels like a shadow. I never knew it to fail. It's just as sure as a stomach-ache is to follow overeating."

source.name: Mother West Wind 'Why' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1915)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What lesson does the storyteller want to teach?
choices: Playing tricks is a harmless way to have fun
Mischief is always followed by trouble
Overeating is the worst thing you can do
Shadows follow you wherever you go
question.evidence: you'll see Trouble following at his heels like a shadow
question.explain: The storyteller says Trouble always follows Mischief.

passages.title: Striped Chipmunk Wonders
passages.text: Striped Chipmunk sat staring at a little ridge where the grass was raised up. He had often seen little ridges like that without thinking much about them. He knew that they were made by Miner the Mole. He had known that ever since he was big enough to begin to ask questions. But now as he looked at this one, it suddenly struck him that he had not seen Miner the Mole more than once or twice in all his life.

source.name: Mother West Wind 'Why' Stories (Thornton W. Burgess, 1915)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why has Striped Chipmunk most likely seen Miner the Mole so rarely?
choices: Miner spends nearly all his time underground
Miner lives far away in the Green Forest
Miner is very afraid of Striped Chipmunk
Miner only comes out when the winter snow falls
question.evidence: a little ridge where the grass was raised up
question.explain: Miner makes ridges by digging under the ground, so he is seldom seen above it.

passages.title: Reddy Fox's Dream
passages.text: By and by Reddy Fox began to dream. He dreamed that he had a nice little brown coat that was waterproof, just like the little brown coat that Billy Mink wore. Yes, and he dreamed that he had learned to swim and to catch fish just as Billy Mink did. He dreamed that the Dear Little Pool was full of little Trouts and that he was just going to catch one when--splash! Reddy Fox had rolled right off of the Big Rock into the Dear Little Pool.

source.name: Old Mother West Wind (Thornton W. Burgess, 1910)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

choices: He woke up warm and dry in his own bed

He rolled off the Big Rock into the pool
question.evidence: Reddy Fox had rolled right off of the Big Rock into the Dear Little Pool
question.explain: Just as he was about to catch a Trout, he rolled into the pool with a splash.

passages.title: Everyone Comes to See
passages.text: Johnny Chuck, over in the Green Meadows, heard the noise and stole down the Lone Little Path to see. Jimmy Skunk, looking for beetles up on the hill, heard the noise and forgot that he hadn't had his breakfast. Reddy Fox, taking a nap, woke up and hurried over to watch the fun. Last of all came Peter Rabbit.

source.name: Old Mother West Wind (Thornton W. Burgess, 1910)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess
